claim: TRPML2 is an endolysosomal cation channel that plays a direct role in chemokine trafficking and secretion from murine macrophages.
source: Here, the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML2 is shown to play a direct role in chemokine trafficking and secretion from murine macrophages.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding as a main result of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ML2-SA1 is the first isoform-selective TRPML2 channel agonist.
source: To demonstrate acute and direct involvement of TRPML2 in these processes, the first isoform-selective TRPML2 channel agonist was generated, ML2-SA1.
evidence: The abstract and results sections describe the generation and characterization of ML2-SA1 as the first selective TRPML2 agonist.

claim: ML2-SA1 directly stimulates release of the chemokine CCL2 from macrophages.
source: ML2-SA1 was not only found to directly stimulate release of the chemokine CCL2 from macrophages but also to stimulate macrophage migration, thus mimicking CCL2 function.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by ELISA data in Figure 5A showing increased CCL2 secretion upon ML2-SA1 treatment.

claim: ML2-SA1 stimulates macrophage migration.
source: ML2-SA1 was not only found to directly stimulate release of the chemokine CCL2 from macrophages but also to stimulate macrophage migration, thus mimicking CCL2 function.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by migration assay data in Figure 6.

claim: Endogenous TRPML2 is expressed in early/recycling endosomes.
source: Endogenous TRPML2 is expressed in early/recycling endosomes as demonstrated by endolysosomal patch-clamp experimentation and ML2-SA1 promotes trafficking through early/recycling endosomes, suggesting CCL2 being transported and secreted via this pathway.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 2 and colocalization data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ML2-SA1 promotes trafficking through early/recycling endosomes.
source: Endogenous TRPML2 is expressed in early/recycling endosomes as demonstrated by endolysosomal patch-clamp experimentation and ML2-SA1 promotes trafficking through early/recycling endosomes, suggesting CCL2 being transported and secreted via this pathway.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by transferrin trafficking data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: CCL2 is transported and secreted via the early/recycling endosomal pathway.
source: Endogenous TRPML2 is expressed in early/recycling endosomes as demonstrated by endolysosomal patch-clamp experimentation and ML2-SA1 promotes trafficking through early/recycling endosomes, suggesting CCL2 being transported and secreted via this pathway.
evidence: The abstract suggests this pathway based on TRPML2 localization and ML2-SA1 effects on trafficking, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Cytokines and chemokines are produced and secreted by a broad range of immune cells including macrophages.
source: Cytokines and chemokines are produced and secreted by a broad range of immune cells including macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation.

claim: Little is known about how inflammatory mediators are released from various immune cells.
source: Remarkably, little is known about how these inflammatory mediators are released from the various immune cells.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Cytokines/chemokines are released from immune cells such as macrophages, B- and T-lymphocytes, neutrophils, mast cells and dendritic cells.
source: Cytokines/chemokines are released from a wide range of immune cells such as macrophages, B- and T-lymphocytes, neutrophils, mast cells and dendritic cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cytokines/chemokines are essential for intercellular communication in both innate and adaptive immunity.
source: They are essential for intercellular communication in both innate and adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Our knowledge of the function of cytokines/chemokines in immunity is much more advanced than our knowledge about how they are packaged and secreted from immune cells.
source: Remarkably, our knowledge of the function of cytokines/chemokines in immunity is much more advanced than our knowledge about how they are packaged and secreted from immune cells.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Understanding how innate immune cells release cytokines/chemokines is important because these factors are indispensable for communication between immune and non-immune cells to coordinate inflammatory responses.
source: Understanding how innate immune cells release cytokines/chemokines is important, as these factors are indispensable for communication between immune but also with non-immune cells to coordinate inflammatory responses (Lacy and Stow, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as rationale in the introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: Secretion pathways vary between different cell types.
source: Importantly, secretion pathways vary between different cell types.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Macrophages lack typical secretory granules.
source: Macrophages for example lack typical secretory granules (Lacy and Stow, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: Macrophage cytokine/chemokine release is mediated by direct transport to the cell surface from the trans-Golgi network (e.g. IL-10).
source: Thus, macrophage cytokine/chemokine release is mediated either by direct transport to the cell surface from the trans-Golgi network (TGN) (e.g. IL-10), by transport via recycling endosomes (RE) to the cell surface (e.g. TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10) (Manderson et al., 2007; Murray and Stow, 2014), or via late endosomes/lysosomes (LE/LY), for example IL-1β (Andrei et al., 1999; Lopez-Castejon and Brough, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Macrophage cytokine/chemokine release is mediated by transport via recycling endosomes to the cell surface (e.g. TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10).
source: Thus, macrophage cytokine/chemokine release is mediated either by direct transport to the cell surface from the trans-Golgi network (TGN) (e.g. IL-10), by transport via recycling endosomes (RE) to the cell surface (e.g. TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10) (Manderson et al., 2007; Murray and Stow, 2014), or via late endosomes/lysosomes (LE/LY), for example IL-1β (Andrei et al., 1999; Lopez-Castejon and Brough, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Macrophage cytokine/chemokine release is mediated via late endosomes/lysosomes (e.g. IL-1β).
source: Thus, macrophage cytokine/chemokine release is mediated either by direct transport to the cell surface from the trans-Golgi network (TGN) (e.g. IL-10), by transport via recycling endosomes (RE) to the cell surface (e.g. TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10) (Manderson et al., 2007; Murray and Stow, 2014), or via late endosomes/lysosomes (LE/LY), for example IL-1β (Andrei et al., 1999; Lopez-Castejon and Brough, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Expression of TRPML2 in different immune cells and tissues has been demonstrated by several groups.
source: Expression of TRPML2 in different immune cells and tissues has been demonstrated by several groups (Cuajungco et al., 2016; Valadez and Cuajungco, 2015; García-Añoveros and Wiwatpanit, 2014; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRPML2 has been shown to be expressed primarily on recycling endosomes and late endosomes/lysosomes by immunocytochemistry experiments.
source: On the subcellular level, TRPML2 has been shown to be expressed primarily on RE and LE/LY by immunocytochemistry experiments (Sun et al., 2015; Venkatachalam et al., 2006; Karacsonyi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Functional expression of TRPML2 in different intracellular vesicles and organelles has not been confirmed by direct and selective patch-clamp analysis.
source: However, functional expression of TRPML2 in different intracellular vesicles and organelles has not been confirmed yet by direct and selective patch-clamp analysis, that is patch-clamping of RE, EE (early endosomes), LE/LY, or other endolysosomal vesicles.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: It remains unclear whether direct and selective stimulation of TRPML2 leads to an increase in cytokine/chemokine release from macrophages.
source: Furthermore, it remains unclear whether direct and selective stimulation of TRPML2 leads to an increase in cytokine/chemokine release from macrophages, and which intracellular trafficking pathways mediate the release of these cytokines/chemokines.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: It remains unclear which intracellular trafficking pathways mediate the release of cytokines/chemokines from macrophages.
source: Furthermore, it remains unclear whether direct and selective stimulation of TRPML2 leads to an increase in cytokine/chemokine release from macrophages, and which intracellular trafficking pathways mediate the release of these cytokines/chemokines.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: The lack of isoform-selective agonists is an important impediment for the investigation of different endogenous TRPML-like currents and their functional impact on secretion, endolysosomal trafficking, or autophagy.
source: One important impediment for the investigation of different endogenous TRPML-like currents and their functional impact on secretion, endolysosomal trafficking, or autophagy, is the lack of isoform-selective agonists.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Currently available TRPML channel agonists belong to different chemotypes, including benzenesulfonamides (e.g. SN-1- or SF-21-type), thiophenesulfonamides (e.g. SF-22-type, including MK6-83), isoindolediones (e.g. SF-51-type, including ML-SA1), isoxazolines (e.g. SN-2-type) and others.
source: Currently available TRPML channel agonists belong to different chemotypes, including benzenesulfonamides (e.g. SN-1- or SF-21-type), thiophenesulfonamides (e.g. SF-22-type, including MK6-83), isoindolediones (e.g. SF-51-type, including ML-SA1), isoxazolines (e.g. SN-2-type) and others (Grimm et al., 2010; Yamaguchi and Muallem, 2010; Grimm et al., 2012b; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Efficacy, potency and selectivity of TRPML channel agonists can vary between species.
source: Efficacy, potency and selectivity of these compounds can vary between species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: None of the currently available TRPML agonists is selective for TRPML1 or TRPML2.
source: Furthermore, none of the currently available TRPML agonists is selective for TRPML1 or TRPML2.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: ML-SA1 activates TRPML1 and TRPML3 in mouse.
source: ML-SA1 for example activates TRPML1 and TRPML3 in mouse, while it activates all three human isoforms (Shen et al., 2012; Grimm, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: ML-SA1 activates all three human TRPML isoforms.
source: ML-SA1 for example activates TRPML1 and TRPML3 in mouse, while it activates all three human isoforms (Shen et al., 2012; Grimm, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: MK6-83 activates TRPML1 and TRPML3 in both mouse and human.
source: MK6-83 activates TRPML1 and TRPML3 in both mouse and human (Grimm, 2016; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 activates all three TRPML channel isoforms in both mouse and human species.
source: The putative endogenous TRPML channel activator PI(3,5)P2 activates all three TRPML channel isoforms in both species and, in addition, also activates the endolysosomal cation channels TPC1 and TPC2 (Chen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012; Cang et al., 2013; Grimm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 activates the endolysosomal cation channels TPC1 and TPC2.
source: The putative endogenous TRPML channel activator PI(3,5)P2 activates all three TRPML channel isoforms in both species and, in addition, also activates the endolysosomal cation channels TPC1 and TPC2 (Chen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012; Cang et al., 2013; Grimm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: More than 80 novel derivatives of TRPML channel activators were generated through systematic chemical modification of known lead structures.
source: Through systematic chemical modification of known lead structures we have now generated the first isoform-selective TRPML2 channel agonist, ML2-SA1. We demonstrate that ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in EE and LE/LY as well as in Rab11+ and Tf+/TfR+ (transferrin/transferrin receptor) vesicles.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in early endosomes and late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: We demonstrate that ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in EE and LE/LY as well as in Rab11+ and Tf+/TfR+ (transferrin/transferrin receptor) vesicles.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 2.

claim: ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in Rab11+ vesicles.
source: We demonstrate that ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in EE and LE/LY as well as in Rab11+ and Tf+/TfR+ (transferrin/transferrin receptor) vesicles.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 2I.

claim: ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in transferrin/transferrin receptor positive vesicles.
source: We demonstrate that ML2-SA1 activates TRPML2 in EE and LE/LY as well as in Rab11+ and Tf+/TfR+ (transferrin/transferrin receptor) vesicles.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 2J.

claim: LPS exposure leads to a strong upregulation of TRPML2 expression in macrophages.
source: In macrophages, LPS (lipopolysaccharide) exposure leads to a strong upregulation of TRPML2 expression, while TRPML1 and TRPML3 expression levels remain unaffected by LPS (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, supported by a citation and confirmed by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: TRPML1 and TRPML3 expression levels remain unaffected by LPS in macrophages.
source: In macrophages, LPS (lipopolysaccharide) exposure leads to a strong upregulation of TRPML2 expression, while TRPML1 and TRPML3 expression levels remain unaffected by LPS (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: Activation by ML2-SA1 was not observed in macrophages without LPS treatment which express TRPML2 only at very low levels.
source: Importantly, activation by ML2-SA1 was not observed in macrophages without LPS treatment which express TRPML2 only at very low levels, further confirming specificity of the compound.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 4A-F.

claim: Direct activation of TRPML2 by ML2-SA1 results in an increased release of the chemokine CCL2 from LPS-stimulated WT macrophages.
source: We also show that direct activation of TRPML2 by ML2-SA1 results in an increased release of the chemokine CCL2 from LPS-stimulated WT macrophages, while TRPML2-/- macrophages show no release increase, suggesting that TRPML2 channel activity is directly linked to CCL2 trafficking and secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5A.

claim: TRPML2-/- macrophages show no CCL2 release increase upon ML2-SA1 treatment.
source: We also show that direct activation of TRPML2 by ML2-SA1 results in an increased release of the chemokine CCL2 from LPS-stimulated WT macrophages, while TRPML2-/- macrophages show no release increase, suggesting that TRPML2 channel activity is directly linked to CCL2 trafficking and secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5A.

claim: TRPML2 channel activity is directly linked to CCL2 trafficking and secretion.
source: We also show that direct activation of TRPML2 by ML2-SA1 results in an increased release of the chemokine CCL2 from LPS-stimulated WT macrophages, while TRPML2-/- macrophages show no release increase, suggesting that TRPML2 channel activity is directly linked to CCL2 trafficking and secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: CCL2 is released via the early/recycling endosomal pathway but not via late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: We further provide evidence that CCL2 is released via the early/recycling endosomal pathway but not via LE/LY.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 5B-E showing no effect on lysosomal exocytosis but enhanced transferrin trafficking.

claim: Stimulation with ML2-SA1 promotes macrophage migration.
source: Finally, we show that stimulation with ML2-SA1 promotes macrophage migration, one of the major physiological functions of the chemoattractant CCL2, one synonym of which is monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by migration assay data in Figure 6.

claim: CCL2 is also known as monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1).
source: Finally, we show that stimulation with ML2-SA1 promotes macrophage migration, one of the major physiological functions of the chemoattractant CCL2, one synonym of which is monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: More than 50 chemically modified versions of the TRPML3 activator SN-2 were synthesized and tested.
source: We first synthesized and tested >50 chemically modified versions of the TRPML3 activator SN-2 (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1 and supplementary materials.

claim: The majority of the SN-2 and SF-51/ML-SA1 derivatives were either inactive, non-selective like ML-SA1, or selective for TRPML3 like SN-2.
source: The majority of the SN-2 and SF-51/ML-SA1 derivatives were either inactive, non-selective like ML-SA1, or selective for TRPML3 like SN-2 (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A subset of molecules displayed a strong preference for TRPML2: ML2-SA1 (=EVP-22), EVP-198, EVP-207 and EVP-209.
source: A subset of molecules however displayed a strong preference for TRPML2: ML2-SA1 (=EVP-22), a derivative of SN-2, as well as derivatives of SF-51/ML-SA1: EVP-198, EVP-207 and EVP-209.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: EVP-198, EVP-207 and EVP-209 showed lower efficacy compared to ML2-SA1.
source: The latter three SF-51/ML-SA1 derivatives however showed lower efficacy compared to ML2-SA1 (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: ML2-SA1 and PI(3,5)P2 evoked TRPML2 activation in late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: In LE/LY, both ML2-SA1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and PI(3,5)P2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) evoked TRPML2 activation while no or very little activation was detectable for TRPML1 and TRPML3.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No or very little activation by ML2-SA1 or PI(3,5)P2 was detectable for TRPML1 and TRPML3 in late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: In LE/LY, both ML2-SA1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and PI(3,5)P2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) evoked TRPML2 activation while no or very little activation was detectable for TRPML1 and TRPML3.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: TRPML1 and TRPML3 were robustly activated by ML-SA1 as a positive control.
source: In contrast, the latter ones were robustly activated by ML-SA1 as a positive control (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: TRPML2 channel activity was detectable in early endosomes after stimulation with ML2-SA1.
source: In addition to LE/LY, TRPML2 channel activity was also detectable in EE after stimulation with ML2-SA1 (Figure 2H and K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2H and K.

claim: ML2-SA1 elicited significant currents in Rab11+ vesicles.
source: ML2-SA1 elicited significant currents in Rab11+ and in TfR+ vesicles (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: ML2-SA1 elicited significant currents in TfR+ vesicles.
source: ML2-SA1 elicited significant currents in Rab11+ and in TfR+ vesicles (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: TRPML2 activity (stimulated with PI(3,5)P2 or with ML2-SA1) increases with increasing, that is less acidic luminal pH.
source: TRPML2 activity (stimulated with PI(3,5)P2 or with ML2-SA1) increases with increasing, that is less acidic luminal pH.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: TRPML1 shows maximal activity in highly acidic luminal pH.
source: This differs from TRPML1 which shows maximal activity in highly acidic luminal pH (Chen et al., 2017a; Dong et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section, supported by citations.

claim: TRPML2 channel function is adapted to vesicles of only slightly acidic or neutral pH such as early endosomes/recycling endosomes rather than highly acidic late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: These findings argue TRPML2 channel function is adapted to vesicles of only slightly acidic or neutral pH such as EE/RE rather than highly acidic LE/LY.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the pH-dependence data.

claim: The strong colocalization between TfR or Rab11 with TRPML2 confirms an important functional role of TRPML2 in recycling endosomes.
source: The strong colocalization between TfR or Rab11 with TRPML2 confirms an important functional role of TRPML2 in RE (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The calculated EC50 value for human TRPML2 is 1.24 ± 0.12 μM.
source: The calculated EC50 values for human and mouse TRPML2 were 1.24 ± 0.12 μM and 2.38 ± 0.01 μM, respectively (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The calculated EC50 value for mouse TRPML2 is 2.38 ± 0.01 μM.
source: The calculated EC50 values for human and mouse TRPML2 were 1.24 ± 0.12 μM and 2.38 ± 0.01 μM, respectively (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ML2-SA1 shows high selectivity over human and mouse TRPML1 and TRPML3 in both calcium imaging and endolysosomal patch-clamp experiments.
source: ML2-SA1 shows high selectivity over h/mTRPML1 and h/mTRPML3 in both calcium imaging and endolysosomal patch-clamp experiments and it does not activate TPC1 nor TPC2 (Figure 1; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: ML2-SA1 does not activate TPC1 nor TPC2.
source: ML2-SA1 shows high selectivity over h/mTRPML1 and h/mTRPML3 in both calcium imaging and endolysosomal patch-clamp experiments and it does not activate TPC1 nor TPC2 (Figure 1; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-F.

claim: A hydrophobic cavity created by specific amino acids in TRPML1 tightly accommodates ML-SA1.
source: Schmiege et al., 2017 found that a hydrophobic cavity created by I468 and F465 of PH1 (pore helix 1), F428, C429, V432 and Y436 of S5, F505 and F513 of S6, and Y499 and Y507 of S6 in the neighboring subunit, tightly accommodates ML-SA1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section, citing a previous study, and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: ML2-SA1 is predicted to bind to the same binding pocket as ML-SA1 in TRPML1.
source: Based on this model, ML2-SA1 (both enantiomers are described, one in Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is predicted to bind to the same binding pocket as ML-SA1 as observed in the cryo-EM structure of hTRPML1 (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by molecular modeling data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Six amino acids (A422, A424, G425, A453, V460, and I498) in the binding pocket are unique to hTRPML2.
source: Six amino acids (A422, A424, G425, A453, V460, and I498) in this pocket are unique to hTRPML2 (highlighted in green; Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The observed binding mode of ML2-SA1 at hTRPML1 is different and appears to be energetically less favorable compared to hTRPML2 due to the observed amino acid substitutions in the predicted binding cavity.
source: The observed binding mode of ML2-SA1 at hTRPML1 is different and appears to be energetically less favorable compared to hTRPML2 due to the observed amino acid substitutions in the predicted binding cavity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by molecular modeling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutation of G425 to alanine was found to selectively abrogate the effect of ML2-SA1, while ML-SA1 was still able to activate G425A to a degree not significantly different from WT.
source: Mutation of G425 to alanine was found to selectively abrogate the effect of ML2-SA1, while ML-SA1 was still able to activate G425A to a degree not significantly different from WT (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: G425 is close to the norbornane ring of ML2-SA1 docked to hTRPML2 and substitution to alanine is unfavorable for this binding mode.
source: G425 is close to the norbornane ring of ML2-SA1 (minimum distance 3.6 Å) docked to hTRPML2 and substitution to alanine is unfavorable for this binding mode (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by molecular modeling data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The experimental data corroborate binding of ML2-SA1 to the ML-SA1 binding pocket and confirm a critical role of G425 in mediating ML2-SA1 selectivity.
source: The experimental data corroborate binding of ML2-SA1 to the ML-SA1 binding pocket and confirm a critical role of G425 in mediating ML2-SA1 selectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis and modeling data.

claim: Only after several hours of LPS treatment, robust endogenous TRPML2 channel expression and activity were detectable in macrophages.
source: We confirmed this finding by qRT-PCR and endolysosomal patch-clamping, revealing that only after several hours of LPS treatment, robust endogenous TRPML2 channel expression and activity were detectable (Figure 4A–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR and patch-clamp data shown in Figure 4A-G.

claim: ML2-SA1-induced currents were detectable in transferrin-Alexa555 loaded, vacuolin-enlarged vesicles from LPS-stimulated bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: In LPS-stimulated bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMΦ) ML2-SA1-induced currents were detectable in Tf-Alexa555 loaded, vacuolin-enlarged vesicles, while no significant TRPML2 channel activity could be detected in non-LPS stimulated BMDMΦ Tf+ vesicles (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: No significant TRPML2 channel activity could be detected in non-LPS stimulated bone marrow-derived macrophage transferrin-positive vesicles.
source: In LPS-stimulated bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMΦ) ML2-SA1-induced currents were detectable in Tf-Alexa555 loaded, vacuolin-enlarged vesicles, while no significant TRPML2 channel activity could be detected in non-LPS stimulated BMDMΦ Tf+ vesicles (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Currents measured in bone marrow-derived macrophage late endosomes/lysosomes with ML2-SA1 after LPS-stimulation were smaller than currents measured in transferrin-positive loaded vesicles.
source: Currents measured in BMDMΦ LE/LY with ML2-SA1 after LPS-stimulation were smaller than currents measured in Tf+ loaded vesicles (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: In late endosomes/lysosomes isolated from alveolar macrophages, TRPML2 currents elicited with ML2-SA1 were larger on average than in bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: In contrast, in LE/LY isolated from alveolar macrophages (AMΦ), TRPML2 currents elicited with ML2-SA1 were larger on average than in BMDMΦ (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: ML2-SA1 elicits robust TRPML2 currents in endogenously expressing cells.
source: These data confirm that ML2-SA1 elicits robust TRPML2 currents in endogenously expressing cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the macrophage patch-clamp data.

claim: Incubation with ML2-SA1 significantly increased secretion of the chemokine CCL2 from bone marrow-derived macrophages after 4 hr and 8 hr of LPS treatment.
source: We found that incubation with ML2-SA1 significantly increased secretion of the chemokine CCL2 from BMDMΦ, both after 4 hr and 8 hr of LPS treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ML2-SA1 did not induce CCL2 secretion in unstimulated bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Importantly, ML2-SA1 did not induce CCL2 secretion in unstimulated BMDMΦ.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CCL2 secretion was severely reduced in TRPML2-/- bone marrow-derived macrophages.
